01.note: When the sons of Rabbi Akiva died, all the Jews came to eulogize them with a great eulogy. As the crowd was about to leave, Rabbi Akiva stood on a large bench and addressed them as 'our brothers, the house of Israel.' He said that even had his two sons been bridegrooms, he would have been consoled by the honor shown them; the people had not come for Akiva the man, since there are many Akivas in the marketplace, but out of respect for the Torah. Their reward was doubled, he said, and he sent them home in peace.
01.why: A teaching says a mourner may not greet anyone in the first three days. The Gemara challenges this with Rabbi Akiva, who greeted the crowd on the day of his loss, and answers that respect for the public is different.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: A Sage whose two sons died; he addresses the crowd that came to eulogize them.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law; the Gemara often quotes one to test a ruling.
A public speech of mourning praising the dead, given at or around the funeral.

02.note: When the wife of Yosef the Priest died, he said to her sister at the cemetery, right after the funeral: 'Go and care for your sister's children,' hinting that he wished to marry her at once. Even so, he did not have sexual relations with her until a long time later. Rav Pappa explains that 'a long time' means after thirty days.
02.why: The Gemara has just taught that a widower must wait three Festivals before remarrying, unless he has young children who need care. Yosef the Priest's case shows that exception, and that he still held back from relations during the thirty-day mourning period.

people.name: Yosef the Priest
people.about: A man whose wife died; he asks her sister to care for the children, hinting he will marry her.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who explains that 'a long time' in the story means thirty days.

terms.meaning: A kohen, a member of the hereditary priestly family descended from Aaron.

03.note: Rafram bar Pappa quotes a teaching from Evel Rabbati, a tractate devoted to the laws of mourning: a mourner may not have sexual relations during his days of mourning. It tells of a man who did so, and after his death pigs dragged away his corpse.
03.why: The Sages had quoted Shmuel that a mourner who has relations is liable to death at the hand of Heaven, and Rav Pappa corrected them that it is only prohibited. This incident, quoted from a mourning tractate, shows how seriously the prohibition was taken.

people.name: Rafram bar Pappa
people.about: A Sage who reports the teaching and the incident from Evel Rabbati.

terms.meaning: A separate early tractate devoted to the laws of mourning and death, outside the main Talmud.
The first period after a close relative's burial, during which a mourner refrains from work, bathing, marital relations and other ordinary activities.

04.note: When Shmuel was told that Rav had died, he tore twelve garments over him and said: 'The man I was in fear of has gone.' In the same way, when Rabbi Yohanan was told that Rabbi Hanina had died, he tore thirteen expensive wool garments and said the same words.
04.why: Shmuel ruled that tearing clothes not done at the moment of most intense grief is not proper tearing. The Gemara challenges him with these Sages, who tore when the news reached them later, and answers that a Sage's death is different, since his teachings keep renewing the grief.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who tears twelve garments on hearing of Rav's death.

people.name: Rav
people.about: A great Sage whose death is reported to Shmuel; Shmuel says he was in fear of him.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage who tears thirteen wool garments on hearing of Rabbi Hanina's death.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage whose death is reported to Rabbi Yohanan.

terms.meaning: Tearing one's clothing as a sign of grief, a traditional Jewish mourning rite.

05.note: When Rav Safra died, the other Sages did not tear their garments over him, saying they had not learned from him. Abaye told them the rule speaks of any Torah scholar, not only one's own teacher, and besides, Rav Safra's teachings were in their mouths every day in the study hall. They thought it was now too late, but Abaye said one must tear as long as the eulogy goes on. When they then wanted to tear at once, Abaye told them a scholar's honor is at his eulogy, so they should wait for it.
05.why: The discussion is working out over whom one must tear one's clothes, including a Torah scholar or one present at the moment of death. The Rav Safra case shows how the rule for a scholar is applied, including when the tearing should happen.

people.name: Rav Safra
people.about: A Torah scholar who died; the Sages at first did not tear their clothes over him.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who corrects the others about tearing their clothes for Rav Safra.

terms.meaning: The beit midrash, the house of study where Sages and students learned and debated Torah.
A public speech of mourning praising the dead.

06.note: When Rav Huna died, the mourners wanted to place a Torah scroll on his bier. Rav Hisda stopped them: Rav Tahlifa had once seen Rav Huna move a Torah scroll off his bed onto an upturned jug before sitting down, so Rav Huna would not have wanted it. The bier would not fit through the door; Rav Hisda refused to let them lower it from the roof or move him to a narrower bier, citing what Rav Huna taught about a scholar's honor, so they broke open the doorway. Rabbi Abba began his eulogy saying Rav Huna was worthy of the Divine Presence but Babylonia prevented it. Rav Nahman bar Hisda objected with a verse about Ezekiel prophesying in Babylonia, and his father tapped him with his sandal to stop him troubling everyone.
06.why: The discussion has been about how to honor a dead Torah scholar, as in the Rav Safra case just before. Rav Huna's funeral gives a series of such rules, each taught from Rav Huna's own practice.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A great Sage whose funeral is described.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who directs how Rav Huna's body is to be honored, based on what he learned from him.

people.name: Rav Tahlifa
people.about: Saw Rav Huna move a Torah scroll off his bed before sitting on it.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Gives the opening eulogy for Rav Huna.

people.name: Rav Nahman bar Hisda
people.about: Rav Hisda's son, who objects to the eulogy with a verse; some say it was Rav Hanan bar Hisda.

terms.meaning: The frame or stretcher on which a dead body is carried to burial.
The Shekhina, God's presence resting on a person, as in prophecy.
The land of the Jewish community in Mesopotamia (today Iraq), where Rav Huna lived, outside the Land of Israel.

07.note: Rav Huna's body was taken to the Land of Israel for burial. Told 'Rav Huna has come,' Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi thought he was alive and said they could barely lift their heads before him in Babylonia; now had he followed them here? Told it was his coffin, they went out to meet it, while Rabbi Hanina (and some say Rabbi Ila) did not. The Sages decided to bury him beside Rabbi Hiyya, and Rav Hagga, who had served Rav Huna and knew his piety, carried him into the cave. There the spirit of Rabbi Hiyya's son Yehuda told his brother Hizkiyya to rise for Rav Huna; when Hizkiyya rose, a pillar of fire rose with him. Rav Hagga, frightened, stood the coffin up and left, and was not harmed.
07.why: The Gemara is gathering stories about the deaths and funerals of Sages and how they were honored. It also uses the Sages who did or did not go out to meet the coffin to reconcile two teachings on standing in line for a coffin passing between places.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A great Sage from Babylonia whose body is brought to the Land of Israel for burial.

people.name: Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi
people.about: Sages in the Land of Israel who had once been in awe of Rav Huna in Babylonia; they go out to meet his coffin.

people.name: Rav Hagga
people.about: Rav Huna's former student and attendant, who carries his body into Rabbi Hiyya's burial cave.

people.name: Yehuda and Hizkiyya
people.about: Rabbi Hiyya's sons, buried on either side of him; Yehuda tells Hizkiyya to rise for Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who spread Torah in Israel; Rav Huna is buried beside him.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: black leather boxes with Torah verses, strapped to the arm and head during prayer; the straps' black side should face outward.
A blessing said in a line formed to comfort mourners as a funeral passes.
Rav Hagga cites never having had one as a sign of his purity, fitting him to enter the holy burial cave.

08.note: When Rabba bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna died, both were carried to the Land of Israel. At a bridge, the camels carrying them stopped and would not move. A certain Arab asked why, and was told the dead Sages were showing honor to each other, each telling the other to go first. The Arab said that by law Rabba bar Huna should go first; Rabba bar Huna's camel then crossed, and the Arab's molars and teeth fell out. A child then opened the eulogy, mourning the 'shoot of an ancient line' and the 'book of wars' come up from Babylonia, and saying God rejoices when a righteous soul comes to Him.
08.why: The Gemara is collecting accounts of how great Sages were mourned and brought to burial, following the stories of Rav Huna and Rav Hisda; famous eulogies follow.

people.name: Rabba bar Huna
people.about: A Sage, the son of a great man, whose body is carried to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage great in Torah, carried to burial with Rabba bar Huna.

people.name: a certain Arab
people.about: A bystander who decides which Sage goes first, and whose teeth fall out.

terms.meaning: A biblical name for Babylonia, where the two Sages had lived.
A phrase from Numbers 21:14 used in the eulogy for Rav Hamnuna, comparing his Torah learning to the book of the Wars of the Lord.

09.note: When Ravina died, a certain eulogizer opened his eulogy with the words: 'Date-palms, hang your heads over the righteous man who may be likened to a date-palm. Let us make our nights like days over one who made his nights like days.' The image is of a man who studied Torah through the night, now wept for through the night.
09.why: The Gemara is gathering famous eulogies for great Sages, following the eulogy for Rabba bar Huna and Rav Hamnuna; the story of two eulogizers who had planned words for Ravina follows.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: A Sage whose death is mourned, likened to a date-palm.

people.name: a certain eulogizer
people.about: The unnamed speaker who gives the opening eulogy for Ravina.

terms.meaning: A public speech of mourning praising the dead, often opened with a short poetic verse.

10.note: Before Ravina died, Rav Ashi asked the eulogizer bar Kippok what he would say on that day. Bar Kippok answered: 'If the cedars went up in flame, what shall the hyssop of the wall do? If the leviathan was lifted by a hook, what shall the fish of the marsh do?' Another eulogizer, bar Avin, objected that 'hook' and 'flame' must not be said of the righteous, and offered instead: 'Cry for the mourners and not for what was lost; it has gone to rest, and we are left with sighs.' Rav Ashi was offended by them, their feet turned crooked, and on the day Ravina died neither came to eulogize him. Rav Ashi said that neither of them could now perform halitza.
10.why: The Gemara is collecting famous eulogies for Sages; this story follows the eulogy actually given for Ravina and tells what happened to the two eulogizers who had prepared their own.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: A Sage who asks the eulogizers what they will say for Ravina, and is offended by their answers.

people.name: bar Kippok
people.about: A famous eulogizer who compares Ravina to a cedar and others to hyssop.

people.name: bar Avin
people.about: Another eulogizer who objects to bar Kippok's words and offers his own.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The Sage whose coming death the eulogizers are preparing for.

terms.meaning: A ceremony releasing a childless widow from marrying her husband's brother, in which she removes his shoe; crooked feet make it impossible, so Rav Ashi's remark is a pun on their injury.
A small, lowly plant, set against the mighty cedar to contrast the great with the humble.
A giant sea creature of the Bible, here an image of a great man.

11.note: Rabbi Hanin was a son-in-law in the house of the Nasi. He had no children, prayed for mercy, and a son was born to him, but on the very day the child was born, Rabbi Hanin died. A eulogizer opened: 'Happiness has been turned into sorrow; joy and suffering have joined together. At the moment of his happiness he sighed; at the moment he was graced, his grace was lost.' They named the child Hanan after him.
11.why: This is the first of a run of eulogies for righteous men that the Gemara lists with a memory aid of names, continuing its collection of how great Sages were mourned.

people.name: Rabbi Hanin
people.about: A Sage married into the family of the Nasi, who died on the day his long-prayed-for son was born.

people.name: a certain eulogizer
people.about: The unnamed speaker who opens Rabbi Hanin's eulogy.

terms.meaning: The president or patriarch, the head of the Jewish community and its Sages in the Land of Israel.
A play on Rabbi Hanin's name, which sounds like the Hebrew word for grace or favor.

12.note: When Rabbi Yohanan died, Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar opened his eulogy: 'Today is as hard for the Jewish people as the day the sun set at noon,' quoting the prophet Amos about the sun going down at noon and feasts turned to mourning. Rabbi Yohanan himself had once taught that this verse refers to the day King Josiah was killed.
12.why: The Gemara is working through its list of eulogies for righteous men; after Rabbi Hanin comes Rabbi Yohanan, whose death is likened to the loss of the most righteous person of a generation.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A great Sage whose death is mourned; he had taught that the verse about the sun setting at noon refers to Josiah's death.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak ben Elazar
people.about: Opens the eulogy for Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Josiah
people.about: A biblical king of Judah whose killing Rabbi Yohanan linked to Amos's verse.

terms.meaning: An image from the prophet Amos for sudden darkness in full day, used here for the death of a great leader.

13.note: Rabbi Abba and Rav Huna bar Hiyya were sitting before their teacher (the text names him Rabbi Abba as well). He needed to relieve himself, so he took off his head phylacteries and laid them on the cushion, and an ostrich came and tried to swallow them. He said that had it succeeded, he would have been obliged to tear his clothes twice. His companion asked where he got that from: the same thing had happened to him, and when Rav Mattana had no answer, Rav Yehuda told him in Shmuel's name that one tears only when a sacred book is destroyed by force, as in the incident with King Jehoiakim.
13.why: Rav Huna had just taught that one who sees a Torah scroll torn must make two tears, for the parchment and the writing, learned from Jehoiakim burning Jeremiah's scroll. This story limits that rule to sacred writings destroyed by force.

people.name: Rabbi Abba
people.about: Removes his phylacteries, nearly loses them to an ostrich, and says he would have had to tear twice.

people.name: Rav Huna bar Hiyya
people.about: Sits with Rabbi Abba during the incident.

people.name: Rav Mattana
people.about: A Sage who had no answer when asked about a similar case.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A Sage who answers the question by quoting Shmuel.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage whose ruling is quoted: one tears only when a sacred book is destroyed by force.

terms.meaning: Tefillin: small leather boxes holding Torah verses, worn on the head and arm; they are holy objects, removed before using the toilet.
Two tears in one's clothing, one for the damaged parchment and one for the holy writing on it.

14.note: A close relative of Rava died, and Abba bar Marta, also called Abba bar Minyomi, came to comfort him. Rava stood the bed upright, as one does for an ordinary visitor, but Abba bar Marta turned it over, treating himself as a close friend. Rava said: 'How lacking in sense is this Torah scholar.'
14.why: A teaching just quoted says a visitor sure of his close friendship with the mourner shares the meal of comfort on overturned beds, and otherwise on upright ones. Rava's remark shows a visitor misjudging that line.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage in mourning for a close relative.

people.name: Abba bar Marta
people.about: Also known as Abba bar Minyomi; a Torah scholar who visits Rava and overturns the bed.

terms.meaning: A mourning custom: mourners turned their beds over and sat or slept on them during the days of mourning.

15.note: When Rabban Gamliel the Elder, the Nasi, died, Rabbi Eliezer told the household to overturn their beds as soon as the body left the doorway of his house. When the tomb was sealed with its cover, Rabbi Yehoshua told them to overturn their beds. They answered him that they had already done so, following the Elder, Rabbi Eliezer.
15.why: A teaching just quoted records that Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua disagree on when mourners overturn their beds: when the body leaves the house, or when the tomb is sealed. This incident shows each ruling given in practice.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel the Elder
people.about: The Nasi, whose death and burial are the setting.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Tells the household to overturn beds once the body leaves the house; called 'the Elder' by them.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Tells them to overturn beds once the tomb is sealed.

terms.meaning: The president or patriarch, head of the Jewish community and its Sages.
The golel, the stone or slab that seals the tomb.
A mourning custom: the household turns its beds over as a sign of grief.

16.note: At first, carrying out the dead for burial was harder on the relatives than the death itself, because of the cost of the burial clothes, until relatives would leave the body and run away. Then Rabban Gamliel set his own dignity aside and was carried out for burial in linen garments, and the people followed his practice. Rav Pappa adds that nowadays everyone is buried even in plain hemp garments costing a dinar.
16.why: The Gemara is listing changes the Sages made to funeral practice out of respect for the poor and the embarrassed, such as plain biers and incense for all. Rabban Gamliel's simple burial is one more change of this kind.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: A leader who chose to be buried in simple linen, and the people followed him.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who says that in his day even cheap hemp garments are used.

terms.meaning: A silver coin of small value; here a sign of how cheap the burial garments had become.

17.note: Rav Hamnuna came to a place called Darumata and heard the shofar announcing that someone in the town had died. Seeing people at work, he said: 'Let these people be under excommunication. Is there not a dead person in town?' They told him the town had separate groups, each caring for its own dead. He said: 'If so, it is permitted to you.'
17.why: Rav had just ruled that when someone dies in a city, all its residents may not work until the burial. Rav Hamnuna's visit shows the rule in action, and limits it where a town is divided into groups that each tend their own dead.

people.name: Rav Hamnuna
people.about: A Sage visiting Darumata who places the townspeople working during a death under excommunication, then permits them.

terms.meaning: A ram's horn; here blown to announce a death in the town.
A ban placing a person outside the community's normal dealings, a penalty the Sages could impose.

18.note: A woman in Rav Huna's neighborhood had seven sons. One died and she wept for him excessively. Rav Huna sent word: 'Do not do this,' but she took no heed. He sent again: 'If you listen to me, well; if not, prepare shrouds for another death.' She did not listen, and all of them died. At last he told her to prepare shrouds for herself, and she died.
18.why: Rav had just taught that anyone who grieves excessively over his dead will end up weeping for another. The story illustrates that warning, and the Gemara goes on to set the proper limits of mourning.

people.name: Rav Huna
people.about: A Sage who warns a grieving neighbor to stop her excessive weeping.

people.name: a certain woman
people.about: Rav Huna's neighbor, a mother of seven sons who mourns one of them excessively.

terms.meaning: The cloth garments in which the dead are wrapped for burial.

19.note: When Rav Yosef turned sixty, he made a holiday for the Sages, saying: 'I have passed the age of karet.' Abaye said to him: 'Even if you have escaped the karet of years, have you escaped the karet of days?' Rav Yosef answered: 'Grasp at least half in your hand.'
19.why: The Gemara has been reading the age at which a person dies as a sign: death at fifty to sixty is death by karet, and sudden death is another kind. Rav Yosef's celebration at sixty, and Abaye's reply, apply both readings.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who celebrates his sixtieth birthday with a feast for the Sages.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: A Sage who reminds Rav Yosef that he could still suffer sudden death.

terms.meaning: Literally 'cutting off': a divine punishment for the gravest sins, here taken to show itself as death before sixty or a sudden death.

20.note: Rav Seorim, Rava's brother, sat before Rava and saw that he was dozing, that is, about to die. Rava asked him to tell the Angel of Death not to torment him. Rav Seorim asked: 'Are you not his friend?' Rava answered that once his fate was handed over, the Angel paid him no heed. Rav Seorim asked him to appear to him after his death, and Rava did. Asked whether dying had hurt, Rava said: 'Like the prick of the knife when letting blood.'
20.why: The Gemara has been discussing what the timing of death means and has turned to the deaths of the righteous; this is the first of several accounts of Sages describing their own deaths.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage on his deathbed who later appears to his brother in a dream.

people.name: Rav Seorim
people.about: Rava's brother, who sits with him as he dies.

people.name: Angel of Death
people.about: The angel who takes life; Rava asks that he not torment him.

terms.meaning: Bloodletting, a common medical treatment in which a small cut is made to release blood; the prick of the knife was a slight pain.
